newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive-Inflationary minefields.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive-Inflationary minefields.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Nov 5 - Just when the ANZ Bank is warning that activity in the housing market could be starting to grow again, Labour and NZ First in their coalition talks may be on the point of throwing petrol on the inflationary fire.
The two parties are said to be joining forces to combat what they see as hefty increases in state-house rents.

Labour leader Helen Clark says that she has raised the prospect of Labour and other parties approaching the caretaker government with a request that it act urgently to cushion the impact of steep rental increases on state tenants.
Ms Clark said her attention had been drawn to the plight of a state tenant in Auckland who was facing a 39 percent rent increase. The family had a five children aged 2 to 8 years.

NZ First campaigned on a pledge to freeze state-house rents for the next three years and increase the accommodation supplement by 20 percent for all low-income people. Labour promised to restore income-related rents for state tenants.

These policies, if they are implemented, could have wide-ranging repercussions in the housing market, particularly in the Auckland region, and add to the woes of the Reserve Bank in its drive to hold down inflation.

If, for example, the principle of market rents is exchanged for rentals based on income, there is likely to be a rush back into state houses from private sector accommodation and waiting lists for state houses are likely to burgeon.
One answer could be to step up the number of new state houses being built.
But there is another problem: many low income people live in private sector accommodation, paying market rents, and getting an accommodation supplement.
They would be worse off, relatively, to those in state housing, since the income-related rents would only apply to Housing New Zealand tenants.
The other difficulty is that many state houses are occupied by tenants who do not necessarily fall into the low-income category.
Would they be evicted to make space for the would-be low-income house-Hungary people? That too would require a change in policy.
One solution to the problem of high rentals would be to increase the accommodation supplement, as NZ First proposes. This would help people in both state and private sector accommodation.

But an across-the-board rise in the supplement might not be the answer, for the level is adjusted according to the cost of housing in different regions. It is for example higher in Auckland that in provincial centres.
Clearly, any variation in policy must be carefully examined: and it is questionable whether the coalition talks can yield a quick-fix solution.
NZ First has to tread carefully in what could turn out to be an inflationary minefield.
Yet it is under pressure from its Maori MPs to score an early policy initiative on behalf of their constituents.
Reports indicate that NZ First is insisting on a detailed and binding contract in its coalition with National and Labour.
It has brushed aside the other parties' efforts to begin with a broad outline of policy objectives.
The contract it wants would demand action on specific policies within a given time frame.

But some Beehive sources say in the new parliamentary environment, it may not be possible to meet target dates of that kind. Legislation is expected to sit in select committees much longer than in the pre-MMP era.

However there are indications that Labour is taking a more flexible attitude on points like this than National, and that has strengthened the impression that the next government will be formed by Labour and NZ First.

But as Micheal Laws, one-time close friend and confidant of Winston Peters pointed out in his Evening Post column, "The moment NZ First makes its fateful decision, then the power will be gone. Like a bee it has one sting, and then mortality".
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
